title: WorldSpeech: A Multilingual Speech Corpus from Around the World
claim: Aligned data is highly uneven across languages and regions, and aggregate language totals decompose into very different country-level sources.
layout: 2 tall panels; left language bars by region, right country breakdown, curved connectors
description: A tall two-panel figure of horizontal lollipop bars on log axes. The left panel has one row per language. Rows are grouped under colored continent headers: Europe, East Asia, Southeast Asia, South Asia, Middle East & North Africa, Americas, Africa, Central Asia and Pacific. Each row has a language label, a dot-capped bar and a value in hours. Values run from about 5,989h for French down to 10h for Xhosa. The right panel is a second set of bars, one per country variant, in the same colors. Thin curved lines link a language dot on the left to its country breakdown on the right. Examples are Dutch to the Netherlands and Belgium, and Arabic to eight countries. Both panels share an 'Aligned Speech (hours)' log axis. The eye goes first to the long European bars at the top.
caption: Aligned-speech distribution across the languages in WorldSpeech. The left panel shows one row per language, with bar length giving total aligned hours on a log axis. Languages are grouped by continent (colored headers). The right panel decomposes languages with multiple country sources into per-country language variants.
abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) performs well for high-resource languages with abundant paired audio-transcript data, but its accuracy degrades sharply for most languages due to limited publicly available aligned data. To this end, we introduce WorldSpeech, a 24 kHz multilingual speech corpus comprising 65k hours of aligned audio-transcript data across 76 languages, collected from diverse public sources including parliamentary proceedings, international broadcasts, and public-domain audiobooks. For 37 languages, WorldSpeech provides more than 200 hours of aligned speech, with 28 exceeding 500 hours and 24 surpassing 1k hours. Fine-tuning existing ASR models on WorldSpeech results in an average relative Word-Error-Rate reduction of 63.5% across 11 typologically diverse languages.
